question: What are the leading thoughts about how to teach computer science to college students in the age of generative AI?

sections.title: Curricular Imperatives and Pedagogical Shifts
sections.text: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the landscape of higher education, necessitating a comprehensive rethinking of computer science curricula [1]. As these technologies become ubiquitous, traditional learning objectives are currently being reexamined to determine their continued relevance in a rapidly evolving field [2]. This reevaluation requires educators to make critical decisions regarding which traditional topics remain essential for a robust education and how to effectively incorporate new skills that are critical in an AI-augmented landscape [1]. Consequently, it is worth questioning the prevailing pedagogical approach that heavily emphasizes traditional fundamentals, such as syntax, semantics, data structures, and complexity, to ensure that the curriculum remains aligned with modern professional demands [1]. The integration of these new competencies is not merely an add-on but a core component of preparing students for a future where AI tools are standard instruments of production.

sections.title: The Gap in Current Academic Offerings
sections.text: Despite the clear need for curricular adaptation, there is a notable disparity between what is taught in top-tier institutions and what is required in the modern workforce. While consistently top-ranked U.S. Computer Science departments rigorously teach the mechanisms and frameworks underlying artificial intelligence, few appear to offer courses specifically focused on the applications of existing generative AI tools [3]. This gap suggests that while students may understand the theoretical underpinnings of AI, they may lack practical experience with the specific tools that are transforming the industry. To address this, a course was developed at a private research university designed to teach both undergraduate and graduate Computer Science students the practical applications of generative AI tools in software development [3]. This initiative represents a pioneering effort to bridge the divide between theoretical AI knowledge and the practical application of generative models in professional coding environments.

sections.title: Industry Standards and Workforce Readiness
sections.text: The urgency of integrating these tools into the curriculum is underscored by their widespread adoption in the professional sector. The extensive use of tools like GitHub Copilot in industry, which is utilized by over 20 million developers, signals that students entering the workforce will need proficiency in these specific technologies [2]. This industrial standard sets a new baseline for employability, suggesting that manual coding proficiency alone is no longer sufficient. Furthermore, the capability of these models is such that if a generative AI model were a student, it would rank among the top performers in CS1 assessments [2]. This high level of performance in introductory evaluations highlights the need for higher education to move beyond basic syntax and focus on higher-order skills, such as system design, critical evaluation of AI output, and complex problem-solving, where human expertise remains distinct from automated generation.

sections.title: Critical Thinking and Ethical Usage
sections.text: As generative AI tools become more integrated into academic and professional workflows, the role of critical thinking becomes increasingly paramount. In the context of scientific writing and research, authors can use ChatGPT as a tool to generate ideas or explore different ways of expressing ideas, but they should not rely on it as a substitute for critical thinking, analysis, and fact-checking [4]. This principle extends to software development, where students must learn to verify the correctness and security of AI-generated code rather than accepting it at face value. The educational goal is therefore to foster a mindset where AI is viewed as a collaborative partner that enhances productivity, rather than a crutch that bypasses the intellectual rigor required for professional competence. By emphasizing these critical evaluation skills, institutions can ensure that graduates are not only proficient in using AI tools but are also capable of exercising the judgment necessary to apply them responsibly and effectively.

question: What are the main challenges in adapting transformer-based models for tabular data representation?

sections.title: Structural and Data-Specific Challenges
sections.text: A fundamental obstacle in applying transformer architectures to tabular data is the mismatch between the model's input requirements and the data's inherent structure. Transformers are designed to process one-dimensional token sequences, whereas tabular datasets are naturally two-dimensional, consisting of rows and heterogeneous columns [2]. This structural discrepancy complicates the direct application of standard attention mechanisms. Furthermore, the heterogeneous nature of tabular data, combined with typically small sample sizes, poses particular challenges for deep learning approaches [1]. These factors limit the ability of models to generalize effectively from limited data points, a problem that is exacerbated when attempting to interpret complex, mixed-type features.

Despite the prevalence of tabular data in practical applications, deep learning models have yet to demonstrate significant improvements over traditional ensemble methods like XGBoost and Random Forests in this domain [3, 15].

While various deep learning approaches, including transformer architectures [9] and hypernetworks [32], have been adapted for tabular data, pre-training and transferring these models to downstream tasks remains challenging [35].

sections.title: Performance Relative to Traditional Methods
sections.text: Despite the widespread adoption of deep learning in other domains, it has yet to demonstrate significant improvements over traditional ensemble methods such as XGBoost and Random Forests in the tabular domain [1]. This performance gap is a critical concern for researchers seeking to justify the computational cost and complexity of transformer-based models. A recent benchmark study on tabular language models, specifically TabLM, reveals that traditional machine learning frequently outperforms large language models on tabular data [4]. This underperformance is possibly attributed to the tabular-to-text serialization required by text-based LLMs, which may distort the original data relationships [4]. Additionally, while small language models work well for general natural language tasks, their ability to interpret tabular data is limited [3]. These findings suggest that simply adapting existing NLP architectures is insufficient for achieving state-of-the-art results in tabular prediction tasks.

sections.title: Architectural Adaptations and Limitations
sections.text: To address these challenges, significant research effort has focused on transformer architectures that can be successfully applied to very large tabular datasets [6]. One of the state-of-the-art solutions is TabTransformer, which incorporates an attention mechanism to better track relationships between categorical features and then makes use of a standard MLP to output its final logits [5]. Building on this foundation, GatedTabTransformer proposes multiple modifications to the original TabTransformer, including linear projections in MLP and gated MLP structures [5]. These modifications have been shown to perform better on binary classification tasks for three separate datasets, achieving more than 1% AUROC gains [5]. However, despite these architectural innovations, pre-training and transferring these adapted transformer models to downstream tasks remains challenging [1]. The difficulty in effective transfer learning indicates that current adaptations do not yet fully capture the necessary representations for robust generalization across different tabular tasks.

sections.title: Emerging Techniques and Critical Gaps
sections.text: In response to the limitations of standard architectures, researchers have recently started applying attention-based methods and self-supervised learning techniques to tabular data [6]. These approaches aim to leverage the strengths of transformers in capturing long-range dependencies and leveraging unlabeled data. However, a survey of deep neural tabular deep learning methods highlights a critical gap: the underrepresentation of latent correlations among data instances and feature values [7]. This gap suggests that current models, including those using attention and self-supervised learning, may fail to fully capture the complex, non-linear relationships inherent in tabular structures. Addressing this underrepresentation is essential for closing the performance gap with traditional methods and unlocking the full potential of transformer-based models for tabular data representation.

question: What are the most important open challenges in Federated Learning?

sections.title: Foundational Heterogeneity Challenges
sections.text: Federated learning (FL) is currently in its prime stages of development, posing several unresolved issues that demand careful consideration [5]. Because the federated setting differs significantly from classical optimization problems, it presents a unique research paradigm [1] [5]. These distinct characteristics create challenges that make FL different from traditional distributed optimization [4]. A 2021 survey identifies the key challenges as model heterogeneity, statistical heterogeneity, communication issues (including system heterogeneity), and privacy [4]. Similarly, a 2025 optimization survey highlights five key challenges arising from the heterogeneity of data and devices, communication issues, and privacy concerns for clients [3]. The 2020 survey also notes that critical open directions remain unexplored regarding expensive communication, systems heterogeneity, and statistical heterogeneity [2]. These foundational issues are compounded by the fact that FL is still a nascent field with many open ends requiring attention [1].

sections.title: Privacy and Security Vulnerabilities
sections.text: Privacy is a central concern in FL, with multiple surveys listing it as a key challenge [2] [4] [3]. A specific 2021 study introduced a novel attack method named Fidel, which reconstructs private training samples from weight updates in regular federated learning [8]. This attack demonstrates that an adversary can recover, on average, twenty out of thirty private data samples from a client's model update when using a fully connected neural network, requiring very little computational resources [8]. Furthermore, the study showed that over thirteen out of twenty samples can be recovered from a convolutional neural network update [8]. In response to such threats, research has explored Differentially Private FL for applications like cancer prediction [7]. The 2020 IoT survey also highlights privacy concerns and communication security as distinct open challenges in that domain [6].

question: What considerations are important for material selection in fabricating industrial robotic grippers?  What are the advantages and disadvantages of soft vs rigid gripper materials?

sections.title: Material Composition and Structural Design
sections.text: The fabrication of industrial robotic grippers relies heavily on the selection of materials that balance compliance with structural integrity. Soft grippers are predominantly constructed from highly compliant substances, specifically silicone elastomers or hydrogels [4]. In many designs, single-mass grippers and fingers utilize silicone or rubber-like materials to achieve the necessary flexibility [3]. These material choices allow the gripper to deform and adapt to the specific shape of the captured object [2]. This deformation capability enables the device to grasp a wide variety of objects that differ in shape, material composition, and fragility [2]. Furthermore, the use of soft and flexible materials permits large retracting motions without the requirement for complex joint mechanisms [1].

sections.title: Advantages of Soft Gripper Materials
sections.text: Soft grippers offer several distinct benefits over traditional rigid counterparts. They possess high flexibility, a simple mechanical structure, short response times, and lightweight characteristics [6]. The inherent properties of soft materials provide good bionic performance, which is advantageous for mimicking natural grasping behaviors [6]. A primary advantage is the ability to handle delicate and fragile objects safely, as the soft materials provide necessary compliance during contact [4]. This compliance allows for a more gentle interaction with fragile items while making the gripper more tolerant to potentially damaging forces [1]. Additionally, soft materials offer shape adaptability when in contact with objects, which is a significant improvement over rigid systems [5]. The safety profile of these materials also makes them suitable for human-robot interaction scenarios [4].

sections.title: Limitations of Rigid Gripper Systems
sections.text: Traditional rigid grippers face several disadvantages that have become increasingly apparent in industrial applications. These systems are characterized by heavy weight, complex structural designs, and high rigidity [6]. A major vulnerability of rigid grippers is their difficulty in achieving a compliant grip when handling fragile, rotten, or irregularly shaped objects [7]. Without additional modifications, rigid grippers often struggle to interact safely with such items [7]. To overcome these limitations, precision sensors are frequently added to improve the interaction ability of rigid grippers [7]. However, the integration of these precision sensors inevitably increases the total cost of the system [7]. Consequently, the combination of high weight, structural complexity, and the added expense of sensors makes rigid grippers less ideal for certain delicate manipulation tasks compared to their soft counterparts [6][7].

sections.title: Challenges and Disadvantages of Soft Materials
sections.text: Despite their benefits, soft materials present specific engineering challenges and inherent limitations. The fabrication of soft grippers often requires an iterated casting process, which is typically complex and time-consuming [3]. This manufacturing complexity is a notable disadvantage associated with rubber-like materials [3]. Furthermore, the use of soft materials introduces inherent limitations regarding mechanical behavior. One such limitation is the slightly unpredictable deformation of the material during operation [8]. Another challenge is the increased nonlinearity of the components, which complicates control and modeling [8]. Additionally, soft materials are associated with low force capabilities, which may restrict their application in tasks requiring high gripping strength [8]. These factors—unpredictable deformation, nonlinearity, and low force output—must be carefully considered when selecting materials for industrial robotic grippers [8][8][8].

sections.title: Industrial and Manufacturing Applications
sections.text: Dexterous robot hands are essential for manufacturing and assembly processes, where they enable precise in-hand manipulation [3]. In industrial settings, these systems address the limitations of traditional equipment; a human arm and hand, possessing more than 30 degrees of freedom (DOF), is significantly more flexible for object manipulation than a standard 6-DOF robot equipped with a simple gripper [2]. This flexibility allows for fast and accurate execution of tasks that meet the rigorous demands of many manufacturing processes [2]. Consequently, dexterous robotic hands have found wide-ranging applications in industrial manufacturing, serving as a critical component in modern production lines [1].

These environments require the ability to navigate and interact with objects without pre-arranged layouts, a capability that dexterous hands provide [4]. Additionally, these systems are applied in the handling of dangerous goods, where remote or automated dexterity reduces risk to human operators [1]. The versatility required for these varied settings highlights the broad utility of dexterous hands in both service and safety-critical roles [1].

sections.title: Technical Challenges and Design Principles
sections.text: Despite their utility, versatile in-hand manipulation remains a long-standing challenge in robotics [4]. The difficulty stems from the high degrees of freedom (DoFs) in the control space and the complex physical interactions between the hand and the object [6] [7]. To address this, researchers design multifingered dexterous robotic hands that mimic the structure and function of the human hand, aiming to replace traditional manipulators [8]. Tasks for these hands are generally divided into two distinct groups: grasping and manipulation [1]. The complexity of controlling such high-DOF systems requires advanced approaches to manage the intricate dynamics of object interaction [6] [7].

sections.title: Advanced Capabilities and Learning Methods
sections.text: Recent advancements have demonstrated the ability to perform complex in-hand manipulation tasks, such as solving a Rubik's Cube, using systems like the Shadow hand [3]. A key technique in this domain is finger-gaiting, which enables large-angle in-hand re-orientation of objects [4]. This capability is often learned through reinforcement learning (RL) using proprioceptive and tactile feedback, allowing the system to transfer skills to novel objects [4]. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has shown particular promise in solving dexterous in-hand manipulation tasks due to its robust learning capabilities [7]. These learning-based methods help overcome the inherent difficulties posed by the high-dimensional control spaces and complex object interactions characteristic of dexterous manipulation [7] [6].
